clips.text_zh: 又係呢句：跟女傭就得。BTC、XRP、DOGE，揸住就得，咁簡單。我連揸都揸唔住，仲輸緊，廢柴。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: BTC, XRP, DOGE — all you literally had to do was follow the maid. That is all you had to hold. The thread on /biz/ tonight mocks anyone who sold early or never bothered buying while the pump was happening.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ OP blames retail for missing the maid-led pump in BTC, XRP, DOGE.

signal.rationale: OP implies the maid-driven basket (BTC/XRP/DOGE) is still the play and retail should have held

clips.text_en_b2: Bitcoin, XRP, and DOGE — anyone who simply held them through the rally made out like a bandit, because the only strategy that mattered was following the maid and refusing to sell. The /biz/ thread tonight is absolutely roasting everybody who dumped early or never bothered picking up a single coin while the pump was unfolding, and honestly, the mockery is not entirely undeserved.
clips.text_en_c1: The thesis peddled across /biz/ tonight is brutally reductive yet, by all accounts, irrefutable: had you simply followed the maid's signals and held BTC, XRP, and DOGE through the rally, you would be sitting comfortably in the green. The thread mocks anyone who panic-sold near the bottom or, worse still, never bothered to allocate a position while the pump was unfolding in real time. Anyone who failed to hold is now reconciling themselves with the stark reality that conviction, however late, would have been profitable. The consensus is unanimous: the trade was obvious in hindsight, which makes losing money on it all the more unforgivable.
clips.text_en_c2: The familiar refrain resurfaced on /biz/ tonight, and the irony is almost too on the nose to ignore: BTC, XRP, and DOGE rewarded nothing more than the patience to hold. That, in essence, was the entirety of the strategy. Yet for every poster who rode the pump to local tops, there were ten others, myself included, who capitulated at the first sign of volatility and now nurse losses while watching the candle rip higher. The thread, predictably, has devolved into ritual humiliation of weak hands and anyone who deigned to short the trend. Mockery aside, the underlying thesis remains deceptively simple: conviction, however inarticulate, outpaced analysis at every turn. Whether that constitutes wisdom or merely survivorship bias dressed up as prescience is a question the board, characteristically, has no appetite for examining.

clips.text_zh: 9,150 DOGE 想溝到 25,000，諗住去到 £1 就買 Toyota AE86。我嘅AE86就係prop firm pass，btw一樣離晒譜。👍
clips.text_en_b1: I have 9,150 DOGE. Should I try to build up to 25,000 in case it does hit £1? I want to buy a Toyota AE86. The OP is asking /biz/ whether the bag is worth topping up.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ OP plans to accumulate DOGE toward 25k to afford an AE86.

signal.rationale: Anon accumulation target is 25k DOGE to buy an AE86

clips.text_en_b2: I am currently sitting on 9,150 DOGE and weighing whether to top the bag up to 25,000 in case it actually reaches £1, because my dream has always been to pick up a Toyota AE86 with the profits. While the rest of /biz/ debates the odds, my personal version of the AE86 is a prop firm pass, which is equally unrealistic, if I am being honest.
clips.text_en_c1: I currently hold 9,150 DOGE, a position I am seriously contemplating topping up to 25,000 on the off chance that the token revisits the elusive £1 mark. Should that improbable scenario materialise, my plan is to liquidate the entire bag and use the proceeds to purchase a Toyota AE86, a car I have been quietly coveting for the better part of a decade. The post on /biz/ poses an ostensibly straightforward question about whether the upside justifies further capital deployment, though anyone familiar with meme-coin dynamics understands that such targets rarely materialise on schedule.
clips.text_en_c2: The arithmetic on display in this /biz/ thread is charmingly quixotic, the kind of napkin math that fuels an entire thread's worth of delusion. I presently hold 9,150 DOGE, and the question animating the OP is whether to top up toward 25,000 on the speculative premise that the token might, against all reasonable expectation, breach the £1 threshold. Should that miracle materialise, the stated objective is prosaic yet oddly affecting: a second-hand Toyota AE86, the car of choice for any autodidact who came of age watching Initial D. Adjacent posters, predictably, have begun performing the same mental alchemy with prop firm evaluations, since apparently passing a funded challenge and acquiring a quarter-century-old coupé occupy the same tier of plausible aspiration. Nobody on the thread has yet mentioned the small matter of liquidity.

clips.text_zh: /g/ 嗰邊話LLM coding一係one-shot，一係寫埋啲subtle bug永遠過唔到review。考牌野我點敢靠AI續命，廢物。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Are there any recent studies that look at whether AI helps SWE or SRE productivity? Feels like current LLMs either one-shot the task or mess it up in subtle ways that would never pass code review. The thread on /g/ questions the real gains.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread asking whether AI actually helps software engineering productivity.

signal.rationale: Meta-discussion on AI productivity, no trade

clips.text_en_b2: Are there any rigorous studies that actually measure whether large language models genuinely boost software engineer or SRE productivity? The general consensus on /g/ seems to be that current LLMs either nail the task in a single shot or quietly introduce subtle bugs that would never survive a proper code review, which is precisely why I would not stake my certification prep on them.
clips.text_en_c1: A thread on /g/ has reignited scepticism over the productivity gains that contemporary LLMs purportedly deliver to software and reliability engineers. The prevailing view is that the technology operates in a disturbingly bimodal fashion, wherein straightforward tasks are dispatched in a single shot, whereas anything more nuanced tends to surface subtle bugs that would never survive a competent code review. Recent studies examining real-world engineering output appear to corroborate the anecdotal complaints that have circulated for months.
clips.text_en_c2: A thread on /g/ has been quietly accumulating steam, its central grievance one that practitioners across the industry have begun to articulate in increasingly weary terms. The empirical literature, insofar as it exists, remains inconclusive on whether large language models confer genuine productivity gains upon software and reliability engineers, or whether they merely redistribute effort. Anecdotally, the consensus that has hardened across the profession is unflattering: contemporary models either resolve a task in a single, almost smug pass, or they introduce defects so syntactically elegant and logically insidious that they evade every line of review. The distinction matters profoundly, particularly in regulated contexts where one's professional licensure hangs in the balance. There is a grim, recurring pattern in which the marginal cost of debugging AI-authored code eventually eclipses the marginal benefit of having generated it.

clips.text_zh: /pol/ 嗰邊話：講一句「亞洲男人平均矮啲」，即刻分到IQ高低。我笑咗，又覺得準，lol。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: The easiest way to test someone's intelligence is to make a generalized statement about a group. Anyone who replies 'not all asian men are short' has just proven they cannot understand a statistical average. The thread on /pol/ is brutal.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ OP proposes a statistical-average IQ litmus test.
clips.text_en_b2: Arguably the quickest way to gauge someone's intellect is to drop a sweeping generalisation about a demographic, because anyone who immediately fires back with 'not all Asian men are short' has inadvertently exposed that they cannot grasp the concept of a statistical average. The /pol/ thread is brutal, but the underlying logic is unfortunately rather sound.
clips.text_en_c1: The simplest litmus test for ascertaining someone's cognitive calibre, at least according to a thread currently circulating on /pol/, is to proffer a sweeping generalisation about a demographic group and observe the reaction. Anyone who reflexively responds with 'not all asian men are short' has, in that very moment, conclusively demonstrated an inability to parse the concept of a statistical average, thereby proving the point far more eloquently than the original assertion could have. The thread is unsparing in its contempt for such responses, treating them as an involuntary confession of intellectual mediocrity.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition floated on /pol/, delivered with characteristic brutality, amounts to an impromptu litmus test of cognitive sophistication. The formulation is disarmingly simple: assert a bland statistical generalisation about any demographic cohort, then observe who seizes upon the exception as though it invalidates the rule. Anyone compelled to respond with the ritual incantation of 'not all X' has, in the original poster's estimation, conclusively demonstrated an inability to distinguish between a population-level mean and the variance distributed around it. The thread, predictably, is less an exercise in statistics than in self-selection, a filter that purports to separate the numerate from the innumerate by means of bait so obvious it functions almost as a shibboleth. The irony, of course, is that the test itself generalises with equal abandon.

clips.text_zh: 2012年30M budget 120人，2026年2B budget 6000人。LOL個first-person mode執咗，唔怪得。lol，S15睇下算。👍
clips.text_en_b1: No wonder first-person mode was abandoned in League of Legends. From a 30M budget and 120 developers in 2012 to a 2 BILLION budget and 6000 developers in 2026. The /v/ thread is roasting the scaling.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread mocks LOL's first-person mode being dropped despite ballooning budgets.
clips.text_en_b2: It is hardly surprising that first-person mode was quietly shelved in League of Legends when you look at the numbers, because the project ballooned from a modest 30 million budget with roughly 120 developers back in 2012 to an eye-watering 2 billion budget and a workforce of 6,000 in 2026. The /v/ thread is roasting the absurd scaling, and frankly, the math speaks for itself.
clips.text_en_c1: Once one considers the sheer arithmetic of League of Legends' development pipeline, the cancellation of its long-rumoured first-person mode ceases to feel surprising and starts to feel almost inevitable. In 2012, Riot operated on a comparatively modest budget of thirty million dollars supported by a team of roughly 120 developers; by 2026, that figure has ballooned to a staggering two billion dollars, with a headcount now approaching 6,000. The /v/ thread savages the studio for what it perceives as grotesque organisational bloat, arguing that any project requiring genuine coordination has effectively been strangled by its own scale. With Season 15 on the horizon, expectations have been duly recalibrated.
clips.text_en_c2: The /v/ thread has settled, with uncharacteristic unanimity, into a single, weary conclusion about the abandoned first-person mode in League of Legends. Stripped of its particulars, the trajectory is nothing short of grotesque: a project that commenced in 2012 with a modest thirty-million-dollar budget and a lean team of one hundred and twenty developers has, by 2026, ballooned into a two-billion-dollar behemoth staffed by roughly six thousand. Proportionally, that represents an order-of-magnitude expansion in headcount accompanied by a far more dramatic expansion in expenditure, the inverse of any plausible efficiency frontier. The feature's quiet cancellation ceases to be mysterious once those figures are juxtaposed, since any genuinely innovative mode would have required dismantling the very bloat that ostensibly justified its existence. S15, it seems, will be endured rather than enjoyed.

clips.text_zh: /fit/ 話大個返office就肥。我而家日頭返工夜晚考牌，gym去到肥仔信都話我瘦咗，wtf。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Why do office workers get fat? The OP says he just landed his first office job and everyone around him is overweight or skinny-fat. He is scared he will end up the same now that college workout time is gone. The /fit/ thread hits hard for anyone grinding 9-to-6.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ OP fears losing his physique after switching from college to office life.

signal.rationale: Body composition lifestyle thread, no trade

clips.text_en_b2: Why does every office worker inevitably end up packing on the pounds? The OP explains that he recently landed his first desk job and has noticed that virtually everyone around him is either overweight or skinny-fat, which has got him worried now that his college training schedule is no longer in play. The /fit/ thread resonates hard with anybody grinding through a 9-to-6 while still trying to hold things together.
clips.text_en_c1: A recurring thread on /fit/ addresses a phenomenon that anyone transitioning from academia to corporate life has likely observed firsthand: the inexorable tendency of office-bound workers to gain weight once their routines stabilise. The original poster, fresh into his first desk-based role, notes with growing alarm that virtually every colleague he encounters falls somewhere on the spectrum between outright overweight and the dreaded skinny-fat category, and he is understandably anxious about succumbing to the same fate now that the unstructured gym sessions of university life are behind him. For those of us juggling daytime employment with evening exam preparation, the prognosis feels especially grim.
clips.text_en_c2: A thread on /fit/, ubiquitous enough by now to have acquired the status of folk wisdom, poses a question whose answer every sedentary professional has long intuited: why does the transition from academic to corporate life coincide so reliably with the metabolically inexorable? The OP, freshly inducted into the nine-to-six, surveys his new colleagues with the horrified recognition of a man surveying his own probable future. The familiar taxonomy presents itself, endomorphs and skinny-fat ectomorphs alike, united in their gradual accommodation to fluorescent lighting and vending-machine cuisine. The poster himself, paradoxically, continues to attend the gym with sufficient diligence that even the uncharitable eye of the trainer has remarked upon his leanness, a development he greets with bemused disbelief. The thread lands hardest, naturally, on those grinding through licensure exams by candlelight.

clips.text_zh: 轉生、cheat、慢生活、惡役，書局同streaming全部係呢啲。Toyokeizai話係外國人帶嚟，我信一半lol。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Anime is no longer made for Japanese audiences. Bookstores and streaming services are flooded with isekai reincarnation works. New releases keep using words like reincarnation, cheat, exile, villainess, and slow life. The Toyokeizai piece blames foreign demand for the plague.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread discussing Toyokeizai article on isekai oversaturation and foreign demand.
clips.text_en_b2: It increasingly feels like anime is no longer being produced primarily for domestic Japanese audiences, because bookstores and streaming platforms alike are absolutely drowning in isekai reincarnation titles, with virtually every new release leaning on buzzwords like reincarnation, cheat, exile, villainess, and slow life. The Toyokeizai piece pins most of the blame on foreign demand, and although I am only half-convinced, the saturation is genuinely difficult to ignore.
clips.text_en_c1: A recent Toyokeizai piece has catalysed debate across /a/ regarding the creeping homogeneity of contemporary anime, which increasingly appears engineered for export markets rather than domestic audiences. Bookstore shelves and streaming catalogues alike are saturated with isekai reincarnation narratives, peppered with the now-familiar vocabulary of cheat abilities, political exile, villainess arcs, and the slow-life subgenre. The article attributes the glut principally to foreign demand, a thesis I find myself half-inclined to accept, given that domestic publishers have evidently decided that these formulae constitute the safest possible commercial bet.
clips.text_en_c2: The phenomenon catalogued across /a/ and substantiated, however tendentiously, by a Toyokeizai feature, has by now acquired the character of an industry in remission from any original impulse. The taxonomy of contemporary isekai proliferation has become almost self-parodic in its comprehensiveness: reincarnation, cheat abilities, exile narratives, villainess reversals, and the pastoral idylls of slow-life variants crowd both physical bookstore shelves and the algorithmic feeds of every major streaming platform. The Toyokeizai analysis apportions blame to foreign consumption patterns, a thesis that half-exculpates the domestic production apparatus even as it implicitly indicts an industry for abandoning its erstwhile audience. Whether the foreign-demand diagnosis survives scrutiny, or merely serves as a convenient alibi for creative exhaustion at home, is a question the thread entertains with appropriate scepticism.
